extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate CS103 students learning how to write mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and checklist for writing conventional, rigorous undergraduate-level mathematical proofs (CS103). Covers structure (assumptions/want-to-shows), variable scope, sentence/paragraph style, and common anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly articulate your assumptions and "want-to-shows."
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should begin by introducing the starting assumptions (what is given) and explicitly state the overall goal of the proof (the 'want-to-show'). These two steps define the start and end points of the argument and should usually be written explicitly when learning to write proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General structure: (1) introduce starting assumptions (often introducing variables), (2) state the want-to-show (the goal), (3) give reasoning reaching the goal, (4) state you reached the goal and end the proof. Exceptions: existential theorems often omit assume/want-to-show; proofs by contradiction implicitly have a want-to-show of 'a contradiction' and typically omit restating it. Grading/readers will look for explicit assume and want-to-show except in these exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof structure
rubrics_metrics.description: In a direct proof, begin by stating assumptions, the want-to-show, and the conclusion in that order; then proceed directly from assumptions to the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example pattern: 'Pick any odd integer m and even integer n. We will show that mn is even.' Follow with the logical steps and finish 'This means that mn is even, as required. QED.' Do not omit the opening assume/want-to-show or the final statement that you have proved the stated goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving by contrapositive, state the contrapositive you will prove, then explicitly give assumptions and want-to-show relative to that contrapositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'We will prove the contrapositive, namely that if m is odd and n is odd, then mn is odd. So choose any odd integers m and n. We need to prove mn is odd.' Conclude by restating the original theorem after reaching the contrapositive goal. Make the assume/want-to-show explicit for the contrapositive version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction structure (omit want-to-show)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs by contradiction always begin with an assumption (the negation) but do not include a want-to-show statement; the contradiction itself is implicit as the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example pattern: 'Assume for the sake of contradiction that ...' Develop logic until you 'reach a contradiction, so our assumption must have been wrong. Thus [original theorem statement].' Do not add an explicit want-to-show in contradiction proofs (it is implicit). Also beware of the 'contradiction sandwich' anti-pattern (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential statement conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: For purely existential theorems (there exists ...), it's customary to omit assume/want-to-show: choose the witness and present it, showing it satisfies the property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To prove 'There is n with property P', simply 'Pick n = 2' and verify P(n). No assume or want-to-show is necessary because there's nothing to assume and the goal is the theorem statement itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make each sentence 'load-bearing.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sentence in a proof should advance the argument by (a) setting up a goal, (b) introducing a new variable, or (c) combining preceding results into something new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a sentence doesn't do one of these three things, it is likely unnecessary and should be removed. This check is applied after a first draft to cut irrelevant high-level remarks or unused facts. Examples of load-bearing sentences: 'We will show that ...' (sets a goal), 'Let n be an even integer.' (introduces a variable), 'Since n = 2k, we see n^2 = 2(2k^2).' (combines results). Exercises and examples in the text illustrate removing unused statements and slimming proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and properly introduce variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever you introduce a variable, explicitly state its name, what it represents, and where it comes from. Variables fall into three types: universally-instantiated, existentially-instantiated, or explicitly chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal variables: phrase like 'let n be an arbitrary even natural number' or 'pick an even natural number n.' Existential variables: phrase like 'since n is even, there is an integer k such that n = 2k' (do not say 'for any integer k'). Explicitly chosen values: 'Let m = 2k^2.' Avoid phrasing like 'for every even integer n' in the middle of a proof instead of asking the reader to pick one. Ensure each variable's scope and type is clear to avoid logical errors (examples and incorrect/correct proof rewrites are provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make specific claims about specific variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in proofs must refer to concrete, specific values (variables) rather than high-level, abstract claims about 'numbers' in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arguments that only give high-level intuition without referring to particular variables (e.g., 'Every divisor of a number divides its square' is too abstract). Rework such arguments to pick a specific variable and derive the claim concretely (e.g., 'Let n be even, so n = 2k, then n^2 = 2(2k^2) ...'). This prevents non-rigorous leaps and hidden errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't repeat definitions; use them instead
rubrics_metrics.description: When a definition is relevant, instantiate and use it rather than re-stating or paraphrasing the definition in a way that obscures its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Instead of rephrasing 'n is even' repeatedly, instantiate 'since n is even, there exists k with n = 2k' and use that equality in calculations. Avoid restating definitions as loose claims; use the definition to introduce existential variables or to justify steps. (The checklist flags repetition of definitions as unnecessary verbosity and a source of weak structure.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in complete sentences and paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be written as flowing English in complete sentences and paragraphs rather than lists or terse, fragmented lines of symbolic manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bulleted/numbered lists of isolated equations or sentence fragments are discouraged. Link ideas together to improve readability and make the logical flow explicit. This is enforced because it matches standard mathematical writing and trains effective communication. Examples show converting a line-by-line list into coherent paragraphs that pass the 'mugga mugga' test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid quantifiers and propositional connectives (no ∀, ∃, →, ∧, ∨, ¬) in written proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use formal quantifier or propositional-connective symbols inside proofs or theorem statements written for this class; express these ideas in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace symbolic notation with natural-language phrases: 'For any integers m and n, if m is even and n is odd, then m+n is odd.' When introducing variables, say 'there is an integer k such that...' rather than '∃k'. The course enforces this as a stylistic and clarity rule; corrected examples are provided contrasting symbolic and English versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'contradiction sandwich'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write a proof that assumes the negation, then proves the statement directly, and finally concludes by noting the contradiction — i.e., don't sandwich a direct proof between contradiction framing that adds nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the 'meat' of a contradiction proof is a direct proof that does not use the negation assumption, remove the contrapositive framing and present the direct proof alone. After finishing a contradiction proof, check whether the argument relied on the contradiction assumption; if not, simplify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mugga mugga test: avoid using math notation as the verb and avoid shorthand symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should have a clear grammatical subject and verb; avoid using mathematical expressions as the grammatical verb or relying on shorthand symbols (∴, ∵) to stand in for English verbs or connectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite lines like 'n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2), ∴ n^2 is even' into full sentences: 'Notice that n^2 = (4k^2), which we can rewrite as n^2 = 2(2k^2). Therefore n^2 is even.' Do not use 'mugga mugga' style fragments. Avoid shorthand symbols except in informal blackboard work; they are not acceptable in written proofs for the class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude immediately when the want-to-show is reached
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you have derived the exact statement you set out to prove (the want-to-show), you should stop and conclude the proof rather than continuing with additional explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anti-pattern: a proof continues after showing 'n^2 is a multiple of three' to restate why the theorem holds — this is unnecessary. Use the want-to-show as a well-defined endpoint so readers know when the proof is complete. Finish with an explicit concluding phrase like 'as required' or 'QED'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable-introduction anti-patterns to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Common errors include (a) saying 'for every even integer n' instead of asking the reader to pick one; (b) introducing an existential variable as if it were universal ('for any integer k where n = 2k'); (c) redefining variables mid-proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct patterns: 'Let n be an even integer' (universal), 'Since n is even, there is an integer k with n = 2k' (existential), 'Let m = 2k^2' (explicit choice). Do not give specific numeric examples where the proof requires arbitrary values (e.g., don't pick m=137 when m should be arbitrary). Ensure consistent scope and avoid reusing names improperly.
